gen3.label: Generation III (Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald, FireRed, LeafGreen)
gen3.howItChooses: Each of its four moves starts at 100 points. Each AI flag the trainer has runs a routine that adds or takes away points. It uses the move with the most points; a tie is broken at random. When it compares damage it uses its own random roll (85-100%), so its estimate can differ from yours.

flags.name: Avoid bad moves
flags.text: Takes points off a move that would fail or do nothing: a move your Pokémon is immune to, a status it already has, a stat already at its limit, and so on.

flags.name: Go for the knockout
flags.text: A move that can knock your Pokémon out is favoured. Otherwise a move that is not its most damaging loses 1 point, and a 4× super-effective move gains 2 about 69% of the time.

flags.name: Expert
flags.text: The largest routine: a judgement for most move effects, such as healing when its HP is low or setting up when it is safe.

flags.name: Set up on the first turn
flags.text: On its first turn, a move that raises its stats gains 2 points about 69% of the time.

flags.name: Take risks
flags.text: Risky moves (one-hit KO moves, Explosion and the like) gain 2 points half the time.

flags.name: Prefer extreme power
flags.text: Moves with variable power, fixed damage, very high power, or no power at all (status moves) gain points.

flags.name: Baton Pass chains
flags.text: Status moves only, and only with a party member left; if it does not know Baton Pass the routine runs about 7 times in 10. Swords Dance, Dragon Dance, Calm Mind and Nasty Plot get +5 on the battle's first turn, -10 below 60% HP, +1 otherwise; Protect +2 unless it just protected; Baton Pass -2 on turn one, then +1 to +3 for its Attack or Sp. Atk boosts; other status moves +3 most of the time.

flags.name: Double battle
flags.text: Double-battle judgement: spread moves, not hurting its partner, and moves that help its partner.

flags.name: Mind the HP
flags.text: Which moves it likes depends on its own HP (above 70%, 31-70%, 30% or less) and then on your Pokémon's; for example, it avoids setting up when low.

flags.name: Sunny Day on turn one
flags.text: Meant to give Sunny Day 5 points on its first turn. A bug in the check (pokeemerald's own comment calls it "nonsense") makes it unreliable.

gen3.neverSwitch: It never switches while trapped (Wrap, Mean Look, Ingrain), against Shadow Tag or Arena Trap (even when it is Flying-type or has Levitate, which should let it), as a Steel-type against Magnet Pull, or when it has nobody left to switch to.

switchRules.name: Perish Song
switchRules.text: Its Perish Song count has reached 0: it always switches out.

switchRules.name: Wonder Guard
switchRules.text: Singles only. Your Pokémon has Wonder Guard and none of its moves are super-effective: it switches to a party member with a super-effective move (2 in 3 chance for each such move it finds).

switchRules.name: Absorbing ability
switchRules.text: The last move that hit it was a damaging Fire, Water or Electric move, and it lacks the matching ability: it switches to a party member with Flash Fire, Water Absorb or Volt Absorb, half the time. If it already has a super-effective move, it skips this check 2 times in 3.

switchRules.name: Natural Cure
switchRules.text: It is asleep, has Natural Cure and at least half its HP: it switches out half the time (before it has been hit, or after a status move); otherwise to a party member immune to or resisting the last move that also has a super-effective move; otherwise still half the time.

switchRules.name: Stays: has a super-effective move
switchRules.text: From here on it STAYS IN if any of its moves is super-effective on your Pokémon (9 in 10 for each such move).

switchRules.name: Stays: boosted
switchRules.text: It STAYS IN if its stat boosts add up to 4 stages or more.

switchRules.name: Immune or resisting partner
switchRules.text: Last: it switches to a party member that is immune to the last damaging move that hit it and has a super-effective move against your Pokémon (1 in 2 for each such move), or failing that one that resists it (1 in 3).

replacement: It picks one of your Pokémon and looks for a replacement in two stages.

First, it ranks its party by how hard YOUR Pokémon's types hit them, most damage first, and sends in the first one that has a super-effective move against you. pokeemerald's own comment notes this is the opposite of what a careful player would do.
If none qualifies, it sends in the one whose moves would do the most damage, worked out as if the Pokémon that just fainted were using them.

flags.text: On the battle's first turn, a weather move gains 5 points, unless that weather is already up.

flags.text: Moves the routine counts as harassing (status and annoyance moves) gain 2 points half the time.

gen4.neverSwitch: It never switches while trapped (Wrap, Mean Look, Ingrain), against Shadow Tag or Arena Trap (even when it is Flying-type or has Levitate, which should let it), as a Steel-type against Magnet Pull, or when it has nobody left to switch to. In Gen IV the check is naive, by pokeplatinum's own comment: an ally's Magnet Pull counts too, its own Shadow Tag does not cancel yours, and it ignores Shed Shell.

switchRules.name: Perish Song
switchRules.text: Its Perish Song count has reached 0: it always switches out. The replacement is chosen the way it chooses one after a knockout (below).

switchRules.name: Wonder Guard
switchRules.text: Singles only. Your Pokémon has Wonder Guard and none of its moves are super-effective on it: it switches to a party member that has one, 2 times in 3 for each such move it finds.

switchRules.name: Nothing works (new in Gen IV)
switchRules.text: Every damaging move it has does nothing to your Pokémon, and it has at least two: it walks its party in order and switches to the first one with a super-effective damaging move (2 in 3 for each such move). If none comes in, it walks the party again and takes one with a neutral damaging move (1 in 2 for each).

switchRules.name: Absorbing ability
switchRules.text: The last move that hit it was a damaging Fire, Water or Electric move, and it lacks the matching ability: it switches to a party member with Flash Fire, Water Absorb or Volt Absorb, half the time. If it already has a super-effective move, it skips this check 2 times in 3.

switchRules.name: Natural Cure
switchRules.text: It is asleep, has Natural Cure and at least half its HP. If nothing has hit it yet, it switches half the time; if the last move that hit it was a status move, half the time. Otherwise it ALWAYS switches to a party member that is immune to the last move that hit it and has a super-effective move against that attacker, or failing that one that resists it. Failing both, half the time. The half-the-time switches choose the replacement as after a knockout.

switchRules.name: Stays: has a super-effective move
switchRules.text: From here on it STAYS IN if any of its moves is super-effective on the Pokémon facing it (9 in 10 for each such move). The code does not skip status moves here.

switchRules.name: Stays: boosted
switchRules.text: It STAYS IN if its stat boosts add up to 4 stages or more.

switchRules.name: Immune or resisting partner
switchRules.text: Last, and only if the last move that hit it was a damaging move: it switches to a party member that is immune to that move and has a super-effective move against the Pokémon that used it (1 in 2 for each such move), or failing that one that resists it (1 in 3). pokeplatinum's comments say 33% and 25%; the code is 1 in 2 and 1 in 3.

replacement: It picks one of your Pokémon (at random in doubles) and looks for a replacement in two stages.

First, it ranks its party by how hard THEIR types hit yours, and sends in the first one that has a super-effective move against you. The score is stored in a single byte, so a strong matchup overflows: a 4× matchup counts as 65 instead of 320, and the wrong Pokémon can come in (pokeplatinum's documented "Post-KO Switch-In AI Scoring Overflow").
If none qualifies, it sends in the one whose best move would do the most damage (highest roll, no critical hit), worked out as if the Pokémon that just fainted were using it.
items: Each turn it decides in this order: switch, then use an item, then attack. So a turn it switches is never a turn it heals.

Its first item can be used at any time. Each later one unlocks only as its team shrinks: with 2 items, the second unlocks when it has 2 Pokémon left; with 3 items, the second at 3 left and the third at 2.
Full Restore: below 1/4 HP. A potion: below 1/4 HP, or once it has lost more HP than the potion heals.
Status cures (Full Heal, Awakening and the like): as soon as it has that status.
X items and Guard Spec.: only on the turn its Pokémon came in (Guard Spec. only without Mist). The code's comment says the opposite; the code is what runs.
playbook: It will not switch out while it has a super-effective move on what you have in (9 in 10 per move), or after +4 or more in boosts. Bring something it cannot hit super-effectively and it starts to think about switching.

A Pokémon that is immune to every attack it has (it needs two or more) makes it switch to a counter 2 times in 3, often more. Expect the counter: it is the first party member, in party order, with a super-effective attack on you.

After you hit it with an attack, it may switch to a party member immune to that attack (1 in 2 per super-effective move) or that resists it (1 in 3). The one that comes in has a super-effective move on the Pokémon that hit it.
Hitting it with Fire, Water or Electric when it has Flash Fire, Water Absorb or Volt Absorb in the back invites that Pokémon in, half the time.

After a knockout it sends in the Pokémon whose TYPES hit yours hardest and that has a super-effective move; failing that, the one whose best move does the most damage to you. Because the score is one byte, a 4× matchup can lose to a 2× one.
It never switches when trapped (Mean Look, Wrap and the like, Shadow Tag, Arena Trap, Magnet Pull on a Steel-type).
bugs: Basic checks Levitate where it should check Dry Skin, so it does not know a Dry Skin Pokémon absorbs Water moves (pokeplatinum's own comment).

platinum-kaizo.changes:
-Dry Skin AI Bug fixed
-Moves except Head Smash with the "1/2 recoil" (Draco Meteor, Hyper Beam, Giga Impact, etc.) effect will now follow the intended recoil routine, instead of having bugged targeting
-Moves with the "1/4 recoil" effect (Brave Bird, Close Combat, Take Down) will now use the following routine:

{ If the opponent resists or is immune to the attack, Score DOWN 1. 
  if the attacker is slower than the opponent and the attacker's HP > 59%, Score DOWN 1
  if the attacker is faster than the opponent and the attacker's HP > 40%, Score DOWN 1  }

-"Triple Axel" and "Fury Cutter" both use the Vanilla Triple Kick effect. However, both will be considered "Risky" moves. This does NOT apply to Triple Kick or Rock Wrecker.
NOTE: Hurricane does NOT use the Thunder routine, despite using a similar accuracy check.

Please check individual move index effects/priority, as these can effect the outcomes of the enemy AI.

NOTE: If exported directly from the game, certain moves may read as having effects they do not. This is intentional.
platinum-kaizo.changesNote: From the Mastersheet's "AI Changes" tab, in the authors' words. The authors' pinned summary in the pChal Discord adds: "Left Side Doubles AI does not exist for most Double Battles (it is used on purpose in some cases, marked in docs)", and that ¼-recoil moves use vanilla Superpower's routine. So the Dry Skin bug listed under the engine below is fixed in this hack.
platinum-kaizo.flagSource: The Mastersheet's split tabs, which mark each trainer's flags with icons. A trainer the sheet marks "Left Side AI" is tagged so on the Trainers tab.

emerald-kaizo.changesNote: No published source documents Emerald Kaizo's AI or which flags its trainers have. The engine below is Emerald's; any change the hack makes to it is not documented.

firered-omega.changesNote: No published source documents FireRed Omega's AI. The engine below is FireRed's.

run-and-bun.changesNote: Run & Bun runs on pokeemerald-expansion, whose AI was rewritten in C with its own, much larger set of flags (smart switching, knowing your party, predicting switches, and more). Which version of it Run & Bun uses, and which flags its trainers have, are not in dekzeh's public data, so this page does not guess. hzla's Run & Bun calculator models its switch-ins.

radical-red.changesNote: Radical Red replaces FireRed's battle engine, and its trainer AI with it. No public source HoopaDex can read documents that AI or which flags its trainers have, so this page does not describe FireRed's as if it were Radical Red's.
